claim: Perceptual inference requires the integration of visual features through recurrent processing, the dynamic exchange of information between higher- and lower-level cortical regions.
source: Perceptual inference requires the integration of visual features through recurrent processing, the dynamic exchange of information between higher- and lower-level cortical regions.
evidence: This is a foundational claim stated in the abstract, drawing on established scientific understanding of perceptual processing.

claim: Animal research has demonstrated a crucial role of NMDA receptors in recurrent processing.
source: While animal research has demonstrated a crucial role of NMDA receptors in recurrent processing, establishing a causal link between NMDA receptors and recurrent processing in humans has remained challenging.
evidence: This claim references prior animal research findings, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Memantine selectively improved decoding of the Kanizsa illusion in two experiments involving different participants and visual tasks.
source: In two experiments involving different participants and visual tasks, we found that memantine selectively improved decoding of the Kanizsa illusion, known to depend on recurrent processing, while leaving decoding of contrast and collinearity largely unaffected.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2, 3, and 5.

claim: The Kanizsa illusion is known to depend on recurrent processing.
source: In two experiments involving different participants and visual tasks, we found that memantine selectively improved decoding of the Kanizsa illusion, known to depend on recurrent processing, while leaving decoding of contrast and collinearity largely unaffected.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on the Kanizsa illusion.

claim: Memantine left decoding of contrast and collinearity largely unaffected.
source: In two experiments involving different participants and visual tasks, we found that memantine selectively improved decoding of the Kanizsa illusion, known to depend on recurrent processing, while leaving decoding of contrast and collinearity largely unaffected.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2, 3, and 5.

claim: Memantine was only effective when the stimulus was attended and consciously accessed.
source: Interestingly, the results from an attentional blink (experiment 1) and task-relevance manipulation (experiment 2) showed that memantine was only effective when the stimulus was attended and consciously accessed.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental manipulations and results shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: NMDA inhibition through memantine enhances recurrent processing, especially for attended objects.
source: These findings suggest that NMDA inhibition through memantine enhances recurrent processing, especially for attended objects, and thereby provide a crucial step toward bridging animal and human research, shedding light on the neural mechanisms underpinning perceptual inference and conscious perception.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Different theories of consciousness converge on a central principle: consciousness entails integration of information through recurrent neural processes that exceeds the capabilities of mere feedforward processing.
source: Different theories of consciousness converge on a central principle: consciousness entails integration of information through recurrent neural processes that exceeds the capabilities of mere feedforward processing (Mashour et al., 2020; Seth and Bayne, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work on consciousness.

claim: Recurrent neural mechanisms encompass feedback connections between higher- and lower-order cortical areas as well as lateral connections within sensory areas.
source: Recurrent neural mechanisms encompass feedback connections between higher- and lower-order cortical areas as well as lateral connections within sensory areas.
evidence: This is a definitional claim based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Studies in mice and monkeys have revealed a causal role of feedback from higher cortical areas to sensory areas for tactile perception.
source: Studies in mice and monkeys have revealed a causal role of feedback from higher cortical areas to sensory areas for tactile perception (Manita et al., 2015; Sachidhanandam et al., 2013; Takahashi et al., 2016), detection of odors (Allen et al., 2017), and visual stimulus attributes (Ciceri et al., 2023; Lamme et al., 1998; van Vugt et al., 2018; Zatka-Haas et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal research studies.

claim: Studies in mice and monkeys have revealed a causal role of feedback from higher cortical areas to sensory areas for detection of odors.
source: Studies in mice and monkeys have revealed a causal role of feedback from higher cortical areas to sensory areas for tactile perception (Manita et al., 2015; Sachidhanandam et al., 2013; Takahashi et al., 2016), detection of odors (Allen et al., 2017), and visual stimulus attributes (Ciceri et al., 2023; Lamme et al., 1998; van Vugt et al., 2018; Zatka-Haas et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal research studies.

claim: Studies in mice and monkeys have revealed a causal role of feedback from higher cortical areas to sensory areas for visual stimulus attributes.
source: Studies in mice and monkeys have revealed a causal role of feedback from higher cortical areas to sensory areas for tactile perception (Manita et al., 2015; Sachidhanandam et al., 2013; Takahashi et al., 2016), detection of odors (Allen et al., 2017), and visual stimulus attributes (Ciceri et al., 2023; Lamme et al., 1998; van Vugt et al., 2018; Zatka-Haas et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal research studies.

claim: In macaques, general anesthetics targeted at reducing the overall level of consciousness reduce global cortical recurrent interactions.
source: In macaques, general anesthetics targeted at reducing the overall level of consciousness of the animal reduce global cortical recurrent interactions (Mashour and Hudetz, 2018) and block feedback connections to V1, while sparing feedforward processing (Lamme et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to macaque studies.

claim: In macaques, general anesthetics block feedback connections to V1, while sparing feedforward processing.
source: In macaques, general anesthetics targeted at reducing the overall level of consciousness of the animal reduce global cortical recurrent interactions (Mashour and Hudetz, 2018) and block feedback connections to V1, while sparing feedforward processing (Lamme et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to macaque studies.

claim: NMDA has a slower time constant than most other receptors with a decay time constant of approximately 100 ms and is voltage-gated.
source: NMDA has a slower time constant than most other receptors (decay time constant ~100 ms, voltage-gated) and is known to be densely populated in recurrent connections in the cortex (Wang, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on NMDA receptor properties.

claim: NMDA receptors are known to be densely populated in recurrent connections in the cortex.
source: NMDA has a slower time constant than most other receptors (decay time constant ~100 ms, voltage-gated) and is known to be densely populated in recurrent connections in the cortex (Wang, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In macaque monkeys, blocking NMDA receptors selectively disrupted late onset modulations of neural activity in V1 during figure-ground detection.
source: In macaque monkeys, blocking NMDA receptors selectively disrupted late onset modulations of neural activity in V1 (i.e., recurrent processing) during figure-ground detection, whereas blocking AMPA receptors did not, but instead reduced the strength of the first feedforward sweep (Self et al., 2012; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to macaque studies.

claim: In macaque monkeys, blocking AMPA receptors did not disrupt late onset modulations of neural activity in V1 during figure-ground detection, but instead reduced the strength of the first feedforward sweep.
source: In macaque monkeys, blocking NMDA receptors selectively disrupted late onset modulations of neural activity in V1 (i.e., recurrent processing) during figure-ground detection, whereas blocking AMPA receptors did not, but instead reduced the strength of the first feedforward sweep (Self et al., 2012; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to macaque studies.

claim: Feedback connections target neuronal synapses that are rich in NMDA receptors.
source: This suggests that feedback connections target neuronal synapses that are rich in NMDA receptors (among other receptors), whereas feedforward connections target synapses especially rich in AMPA receptors (Thiele, 2012; Thiele and Bellgrove, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents an inference from the cited studies.

claim: Feedforward connections target synapses especially rich in AMPA receptors.
source: This suggests that feedback connections target neuronal synapses that are rich in NMDA receptors (among other receptors), whereas feedforward connections target synapses especially rich in AMPA receptors (Thiele, 2012; Thiele and Bellgrove, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents an inference from the cited studies.

claim: In mice, blocking NMDA receptors strongly reduced hit rates for the detection of whisker movements.
source: In mice, blocking NMDA receptors strongly reduced hit rates for the detection of whisker movements (Sachidhanandam et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a mouse study.

claim: Blocking NMDA receptors via administration of ketamine resulted in impaired feature integration in a texture discrimination task.
source: Blocking NMDA receptors via administration of ketamine resulted in impaired feature integration in a texture discrimination task (Meuwese et al., 2013) and a distortion of the neural representations of objects in early visual cortex (van Loon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a human study using ketamine.

claim: Blocking NMDA receptors via administration of ketamine resulted in a distortion of the neural representations of objects in early visual cortex.
source: Blocking NMDA receptors via administration of ketamine resulted in impaired feature integration in a texture discrimination task (Meuwese et al., 2013) and a distortion of the neural representations of objects in early visual cortex (van Loon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a human study using ketamine.

claim: Ketamine has rather broad adverse side effects, such as sedation and dissociation.
source: Ketamine has rather broad adverse side effects, such as sedation and dissociation, which could potentially explain the observed behavioral deficits and neural distortions.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about ketamine's pharmacological profile.

claim: Ketamine is known for its complex pharmacological dynamics, having effects on several neurotransmitter systems, including catecholaminergic, cholinergic, nicotinic, muscarinic, and GABAergic receptors.
source: Also, ketamine is known for its complex pharmacological dynamics, having effects on several neurotransmitter systems, including catecholaminergic, cholinergic, nicotinic, muscarinic, and GABAergic receptors (Kocsis et al., 2013; Mathew et al., 2012; Müller et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to pharmacological studies.

claim: The processing of collinearity of line elements predominantly relies on lateral connections.
source: The processing of collinearity of line elements predominantly relies on lateral connections (Bosking et al., 1997; Gilbert and Wiesel, 1979; Li, 1998; Liang et al., 2017; Schmidt et al., 1997; Stettler et al., 2002), while processing of the illusory surface of the Kanizsa illusion relies on feedback connections (Halgren et al., 2003; Kok et al., 2016; Kok and de Lange, 2014; Lee and Nguyen, 2001; Pak et al., 2020; Wokke et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroscience research.

claim: Processing of the illusory surface of the Kanizsa illusion relies on feedback connections.
source: The processing of collinearity of line elements predominantly relies on lateral connections (Bosking et al., 1997; Gilbert and Wiesel, 1979; Li, 1998; Liang et al., 2017; Schmidt et al., 1997; Stettler et al., 2002), while processing of the illusory surface of the Kanizsa illusion relies on feedback connections (Halgren et al., 2003; Kok et al., 2016; Kok and de Lange, 2014; Lee and Nguyen, 2001; Pak et al., 2020; Wokke et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroscience research.

claim: Multivariate EEG decoding of the presence/absence of the illusionary Kanizsa triangle served as a marker of feedback processing.
source: Therefore, multivariate EEG decoding of the presence/absence of the illusionary Kanizsa triangle served as a marker of feedback processing (Fahrenfort et al., 2017; Noorman et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing this methodology.

claim: Collinearity decoding served as a marker of lateral processing.
source: The ancillary features of the stimulus, the two-legged white circles, could be aligned to form a non-illusionary triangle, enabling us to use collinearity decoding as a marker of lateral processing.
evidence: This is a methodological claim based on the experimental design and prior validation work.

claim: Local contrast decoding served as a marker of feedforward processing.
source: Because local contrast differences are processed early in the visual system, this allowed us to employ local contrast decoding as a marker of feedforward processing.
evidence: This is a methodological claim based on the experimental design and established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: The decoding profiles of features of different complexities at different points in time, in combination with the associated topography, can serve as EEG markers of feedforward, lateral, and feedback processes.
source: In recent work, we have validated that the decoding profiles of these features of different complexities at different points in time, in combination with the associated topography, can indeed serve as EEG markers of feedforward, lateral, and feedback processes (Fahrenfort et al., 2017; Noorman et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior validation work.

claim: Memantine is a low-affinity, voltage-dependent, uncompetitive NMDA antagonist.
source: We tested how these neural markers were affected by memantine, a low-affinity, voltage-dependent, uncompetitive NMDA antagonist.
evidence: This is a factual description of memantine's pharmacological properties.

claim: Memantine is well tolerated and has minimal side effects compared to ketamine.
source: Memantine is well tolerated and has minimal side effects compared to ketamine.
evidence: This claim is based on established pharmacological knowledge and is supported by the VAS data in the study.

claim: The only significant effect of memantine on subjective state was a moderate decrease in the category 'calmness' compared to placebo in experiment 1.
source: The only significant effect was a moderate decrease in the category 'calmness' for memantine compared to placebo (t28 = −23.07, p = 0.005, BF10 = 8.71; Figure 1C, for details see Methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of VAS data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In experiment 2, none of the subjective measures differed between memantine and placebo.
source: Note that in experiment 2 (Figure 4), none of these subjective measures differed between memantine and placebo, indicating that overall subjective side effects of memantine were minimal.
evidence: This claim is supported by VAS data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Masking drastically reduced T2 visibility in experiment 1.
source: Our masking procedure was highly effective, leading to poor T2 performance on masked trials (red lines in Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The attentional blink was effective, leading to a sharp drop in T2 performance on short lag versus long lag trials.
source: The AB was also effective, leading to a sharp drop in T2 performance on short lag versus long lag trials (green lines in Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Memantine had no effect on perceptual sensitivity in experiment 1.
source: Memantine had, however, no effect on perceptual sensitivity (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Local contrast decoding accuracy peaked at 86 ms after stimulus onset in the training data of experiment 1.
source: Local contrast, collinearity, and illusion decoding accuracy peaked at 86, 242, and 273 ms after stimulus onset, and these peaks were encompassed by a 78–94, 192–292, and 223–323 ms time window, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Collinearity decoding accuracy peaked at 242 ms after stimulus onset in the training data of experiment 1.
source: Local contrast, collinearity, and illusion decoding accuracy peaked at 86, 242, and 273 ms after stimulus onset, and these peaks were encompassed by a 78–94, 192–292, and 223–323 ms time window, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Illusion decoding accuracy peaked at 273 ms after stimulus onset in the training data of experiment 1.
source: Local contrast, collinearity, and illusion decoding accuracy peaked at 86, 242, and 273 ms after stimulus onset, and these peaks were encompassed by a 78–94, 192–292, and 223–323 ms time window, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The timing and mostly occipital nature of the decoding time windows were consistent with the neural processes they are thought to reflect.
source: The timing and mostly occipital nature (see the covariance/class separability maps of Figure 2A; Haufe et al., 2014) of these windows were consistent with the neural processes they are thought to reflect and in line with our previous EEG decoding studies (Fahrenfort et al., 2017; Noorman et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by the topographic maps in Figure 2A and citations to prior work.

claim: Only illusion decoding showed a significant cluster ranging from 211 to 352 ms after stimulus onset for T1 in experiment 1.
source: Crucially, only illusion decoding showed a significant cluster ranging from 211 to 352 ms after stimulus onset (Figure 2A, blue lines).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-based permutation testing results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Memantine significantly improved overall T1 decoding in experiment 1.
source: Memantine significantly improved overall T1 decoding (F1,28 = 8.33, p = 0.007) and drug interacted with visual feature (F1,28 = 5.16, p = 0.011).
evidence: This claim is supported by ANOVA results on time window-based analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Drug interacted with visual feature for T1 decoding in experiment 1.
source: Memantine significantly improved overall T1 decoding (F1,28 = 8.33, p = 0.007) and drug interacted with visual feature (F1,28 = 5.16, p = 0.011).
evidence: This claim is supported by ANOVA results on time window-based analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Memantine selectively affected illusion decoding accuracy for T1 in experiment 1.
source: Post hoc t-tests confirmed that memantine selectively affected illusion decoding accuracy (t28 = −4.14, p < 0.001, BF10 = 101.92), thus leaving local contrast (t28 = −0.60, p = 0.560, BF10 = 0.23) and collinearity decoding unaffected (t28 = −1.04, p = 0.306, BF10 = 0.32).
evidence: This claim is supported by post hoc statistical tests on data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Recent studies using memantine have mostly observed increases in task performance and/or neural markers of sensory processing.
source: Recent studies using memantine have, however, mostly observed increases in task performance and/or neural markers of sensory processing (Korostenskaja et al., 2007; Light et al., 2017; Swerdlow et al., 2016; Swerdlow et al., 2020), and are therefore mostly in line with our observations here.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior memantine studies.

claim: Local contrast decoding was unaffected by the attentional blink in experiment 1.
source: Indeed, local contrast decoding was unaffected by the AB (Figure 3B), and although it was impaired by masking, the drop in decoding accuracy was numerically small (0.012 AUC on average) and considerably smaller than the effect of masking on collinearity (0.026 AUC) and illusion (0.123 AUC) decoding.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Local contrast decoding was impaired by masking, but the drop in decoding accuracy was numerically small (0.012 AUC on average) in experiment 1.
source: Indeed, local contrast decoding was unaffected by the AB (Figure 3B), and although it was impaired by masking, the drop in decoding accuracy was numerically small (0.012 AUC on average) and considerably smaller than the effect of masking on collinearity (0.026 AUC) and illusion (0.123 AUC) decoding.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both collinearity and illusion decoding were abolished by masking in experiment 1.
source: As would be expected for markers of lateral and feedback processing, both collinearity and illusion decoding were abolished by masking (Figure 3C, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figures 3C and 3F.

claim: The attentional blink exclusively impaired illusion decoding in experiment 1.
source: The AB exclusively impaired illusion decoding, but decoding accuracy for the illusion remained well above chance during the AB (Figure 3E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: Decoding accuracy for the illusion remained well above chance during the attentional blink in experiment 1.
source: The AB exclusively impaired illusion decoding, but decoding accuracy for the illusion remained well above chance during the AB (Figure 3E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: For T2 decoding in experiment 1, memantine increased illusion decoding only when T2 was presented outside the attentional blink and when it was unmasked.
source: Similar to T1, also for T2 decoding, memantine increased illusion decoding, but only when T2 was presented outside the AB and when it was unmasked (Figure 3E, top left, note that masking fully abolished illusion decoding).
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Time window-based analyses showed a significant effect of memantine only when the illusion was both unmasked and presented outside the attentional blink for T2 in experiment 1.
source: Also, our time window-based analyses showed a significant effect of memantine only when the illusion was both unmasked and presented outside the AB (t28 = −2.76, p = 0.010, BF10 = 4.53; Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Masking impaired perceptual sensitivity in experiment 2, most prominently for the detection of the Kanizsa illusion.
source: We found that masking impaired perceptual sensitivity, most prominently for the detection of the Kanizsa illusion, and less so for collinearity and rotation.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: For unmasked trials in experiment 2, performance was at ceiling for all visual features.
source: Note that we employed less strong masking in this experiment than in experiment 1, leading to overall above-chance perceptual sensitivity for the masked trials. For unmasked trials, performance was at ceiling for all visual features (no differences in performance).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Perceptual sensitivity was unaffected by memantine in experiment 2.
source: Perceptual sensitivity was unaffected by memantine (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Local contrast decoding accuracy peaked at 86 ms after stimulus onset in the training data of experiment 2.
source: Local contrast, collinearity, and illusion decoding accuracy peaked at 86, 297, and 266 ms after stimulus onset, and these peaks were encompassed by a 78–94, 247–347, and 217–317 ms time window, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Collinearity decoding accuracy peaked at 297 ms after stimulus onset in the training data of experiment 2.
source: Local contrast, collinearity, and illusion decoding accuracy peaked at 86, 297, and 266 ms after stimulus onset, and these peaks were encompassed by a 78–94, 247–347, and 217–317 ms time window, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Illusion decoding accuracy peaked at 266 ms after stimulus onset in the training data of experiment 2.
source: Local contrast, collinearity, and illusion decoding accuracy peaked at 86, 297, and 266 ms after stimulus onset, and these peaks were encompassed by a 78–94, 247–347, and 217–317 ms time window, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: For local contrast in experiment 2, task relevance had no effect.
source: For local contrast, task relevance had no effect, and the significant drop in decoding accuracy caused by masking was again numerically small (0.010 AUC on average); smaller than for collinearity (0.015 AUC) and illusion decoding (0.069 AUC).
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Collinearity decoding was impaired by masking in experiment 2.
source: Collinearity (Figure 5C, D) and illusion (Figure 5E, F) decoding were impaired by masking and boosted when the corresponding feature was task-relevant.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Collinearity decoding was boosted when collinearity was task-relevant in experiment 2.
source: Collinearity (Figure 5C, D) and illusion (Figure 5E, F) decoding were impaired by masking and boosted when the corresponding feature was task-relevant.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Illusion decoding was impaired by masking in experiment 2.
source: Collinearity (Figure 5C, D) and illusion (Figure 5E, F) decoding were impaired by masking and boosted when the corresponding feature was task-relevant.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: Illusion decoding was boosted when the illusion was task-relevant in experiment 2.
source: Collinearity (Figure 5C, D) and illusion (Figure 5E, F) decoding were impaired by masking and boosted when the corresponding feature was task-relevant.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: Cluster-based analyses revealed that memantine significantly improved decoding only for the illusion and only when the illusion was unmasked and task-relevant in experiment 2.
source: Crucially, our cluster-based analyses again revealed that memantine significantly improved decoding only for the illusion and only when the illusion was unmasked and task-relevant (Figure 5E, top left), thus replicating the results from experiment 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-based permutation testing results shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Time window-based analysis revealed an overall main effect of drug for illusion decoding in experiment 2.
source: Also, the time window-based analysis revealed an overall main effect of drug for illusion decoding, and post hoc tests revealed that the drug effect was only significant when the illusion was unmasked and task-relevant (post hoc t-tests comparing memantine vs. placebo, t28 = −3.36, p = 0.002, BF10 = 15.66; Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ANOVA results on data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The drug effect on illusion decoding was only significant when the illusion was unmasked and task-relevant in experiment 2.
source: Also, the time window-based analysis revealed an overall main effect of drug for illusion decoding, and post hoc tests revealed that the drug effect was only significant when the illusion was unmasked and task-relevant (post hoc t-tests comparing memantine vs. placebo, t28 = −3.36, p = 0.002, BF10 = 15.66; Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by post hoc statistical tests on data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Time window-based ANOVAs revealed a main effect of memantine on collinearity decoding in experiment 2.
source: Our time window-based ANOVAs now also revealed a main effect of memantine on collinearity decoding (Figure 5D), in line with the hypothesized role of NMDA receptors in recurrent (feedback and lateral) processing.
evidence: This claim is supported by ANOVA results on data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The approach relied on using EEG decoding of different stimulus features at different points in time, together with their topography, as markers of distinct neural processes.
source: Our approach relied on using EEG decoding of different stimulus features at different points in time, together with their topography, as markers of distinct neural processes.
evidence: This is a methodological claim describing the study's approach.

claim: Non-invasive, indirect measures of neural activity cannot provide direct evidence for feedforward vs. recurrent processes.
source: Although such non-invasive, indirect measures of neural activity cannot provide direct evidence for feedforward vs. recurrent processes, the timing, topography, and susceptibility to masking of the decoding signatures obtained in the present study are consistent with neurophysiology (e.g., Bosking et al., 1997; Kandel et al., 2000; Lamme and Roelfsema, 2000; Lee and Nguyen, 2001; Liang et al., 2017; Pak et al., 2020), as well as with our previous work (Fahrenfort et al., 2017; Noorman et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of methodological limitations.

claim: The timing, topography, and susceptibility to masking of the decoding signatures obtained in the present study are consistent with neurophysiology.
source: Although such non-invasive, indirect measures of neural activity cannot provide direct evidence for feedforward vs. recurrent processes, the timing, topography, and susceptibility to masking of the decoding signatures obtained in the present study are consistent with neurophysiology (e.g., Bosking et al., 1997; Kandel et al., 2000; Lamme and Roelfsema, 2000; Lee and Nguyen, 2001; Liang et al., 2017; Pak et al., 2020), as well as with our previous work (Fahrenfort et al., 2017; Noorman et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiology studies and prior work.

claim: The specificity of the effect of memantine on the EEG marker of illusion-related feedback processing is broadly consistent with previous studies indicating that ketamine affects perception and neural coding in visual tasks thought to rely on recurrent mechanisms.
source: The specificity of the effect of memantine on our EEG marker of illusion-related feedback processing is broadly consistent with previous studies indicating that ketamine, another NMDA receptor antagonist, affects perception and neural coding in visual tasks thought to rely on recurrent mechanisms (Meuwese et al., 2013; van Loon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior ketamine studies and comparison with current findings.

claim: The effect of ketamine in previous studies likely affected intra-area lateral connections in early visual cortex.
source: The effect of ketamine in these studies likely affected intra-area lateral connections in early visual cortex (Meuwese et al., 2013) and inter-area feedback mechanisms (van Loon et al., 2016), respectively.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on cited studies.

claim: The effect of ketamine in previous studies likely affected inter-area feedback mechanisms.
source: The effect of ketamine in these studies likely affected intra-area lateral connections in early visual cortex (Meuwese et al., 2013) and inter-area feedback mechanisms (van Loon et al., 2016), respectively.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on cited studies.

claim: Both memantine and ketamine are known to inhibit NMDA receptors by occupying the receptor's ion channel and thereby blocking current flow.
source: Although both drugs are known to inhibit NMDA receptors by occupying the receptor's ion channel and are thereby blocking current flow (Glasgow et al., 2017; Molina et al., 2020), the drugs have different actions at receptors other than NMDA, with ketamine acting on dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2 receptors, and memantine inhibiting several subtypes of the acetylcholine (ACh) receptor as well as serotonin 5-HT3 receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to pharmacological studies.

claim: Ketamine acts on dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2 receptors.
source: Although both drugs are known to inhibit NMDA receptors by occupying the receptor's ion channel and are thereby blocking current flow (Glasgow et al., 2017; Molina et al., 2020), the drugs have different actions at receptors other than NMDA, with ketamine acting on dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2 receptors, and memantine inhibiting several subtypes of the acetylcholine (ACh) receptor as well as serotonin 5-HT3 receptors.
evidence: This claim is based on established pharmacological knowledge.

claim: Memantine inhibits several subtypes of the acetylcholine receptor as well as serotonin 5-HT3 receptors.
source: Although both drugs are known to inhibit NMDA receptors by occupying the receptor's ion channel and are thereby blocking current flow (Glasgow et al., 2017; Molina et al., 2020), the drugs have different actions at receptors other than NMDA, with ketamine acting on dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2 receptors, and memantine inhibiting several subtypes of the acetylcholine (ACh) receptor as well as serotonin 5-HT3 receptors.
evidence: This claim is based on established pharmacological knowledge.

claim: Memantine and ketamine are known to target different NMDA receptor subpopulations, with their inhibitory action displaying different time courses and intensity.
source: Memantine and ketamine are also known to target different NMDA receptor subpopulations, with their inhibitory action displaying different time courses and intensity (Glasgow et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to pharmacological studies.

claim: Blockade of different NMDA receptor subpopulations can result in markedly different and even opposite results.
source: Blockade of different NMDA receptor subpopulations can result in markedly different and even opposite results.
evidence: This claim is supported by the example from Self et al., 2012 discussed in the text.

claim: Self et al., 2012 found overall reduced or elevated visual activity after microinfusion of two different selective NMDA receptor antagonists in macaque primary visual cortex.
source: For example, Self et al., 2012 found overall reduced or elevated visual activity after microinfusion of two different selective NMDA receptor antagonists (2-amino-5-phosphonovalerate and ifendprodil) in macaque primary visual cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a macaque study.

claim: While ketamine diminishes the amplitude of the mismatch negativity EEG response to auditory oddball stimuli, a single dose of memantine enhances MMN amplitude.
source: For example, while ketamine diminishes the amplitude of the so-called mismatch negativity (MMN) EEG response to (auditory) oddball stimuli (Rosburg and Kreitschmann-Andermahr, 2016), a single dose of memantine enhances MMN amplitude (Korostenskaja et al., 2007; Light et al., 2017; Swerdlow et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on ketamine and memantine effects on MMN.

claim: Most studies found memantine to improve learning and to boost perceptual and neural processing.
